name: Learn basic map and compass navigation
blurb: The full skill: orient a map, take and follow a bearing, work out where you are from what you can see, and cope when the terrain disagrees with you.
gear: A baseplate compass with a rotating bezel
A topographic map of somewhere you can walk
steps: Learn to read the map: contour lines, spacing as steepness, the difference between a spur and a re-entrant, and the scale.
Orient the map to the ground by aligning its grid north with the compass needle, adjusted for magnetic declination.
Take a bearing from the map: baseplate edge along your route, rotate the bezel to grid north, then turn your body until the needle sits in the shed.
Follow it by picking a visible feature on the bearing, walking to it, and re-shooting — never by staring at the needle as you walk.
Learn pacing and timing to estimate distance covered, and count paces over a measured 100 m to calibrate.
Learn resection: bearings to two known features, back-plotted on the map, give your position.
Practise handrails, catching features and deliberate offset — the techniques that make navigation robust rather than precise.
tips: Adjust for declination or you will drift, badly, over distance. Check the value for your area and its year.
Keep your thumb on your position and move it as you go. Losing track is what turns a mistake into an epic.
Metal objects — phones, cars, knives — deflect the needle. Step away before taking a bearing.
proof: You navigate a multi-leg course in unfamiliar terrain, in poor visibility, hitting each control without GPS.
